title: Chapter 48 — The First Lowering
paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they seemed at the time, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and with a noiseless swiftness were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat that hung there. This boat had always been considered one of the spare boats, though technically it was called the captain's, because it hung from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bow was tall and dark, with one white tooth evilly protruding from his steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton clothed him funereally, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning all this blackness was a glistening white plaited turban — his own living hair, braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less dark in appearance, the companions of this figure had that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manila islands — a race notorious for a certain devilish subtlety, and supposed by some honest white sailors to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents, here on the water, of their lord the devil, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" he shouted across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a deft, offhand daring unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," Stubb sighed to his crew in a slow, soothing drawl, some of them still showing signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you're staring at? Those chaps in that boat over there? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good enough fellows. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! Long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil take you, you ragamuffin rapscallions; you're all asleep. Stop snoring, you sleepers, and pull. Pull, will you? Pull, can't you? Pull, won't you? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't you pull? — pull and break something! Pull, till your eyes start out of your head! Here!" — whipping the sharp knife out of his belt — "every mother's son of you draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now you're doing something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's opening address to his crew is given here in full because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in preaching the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this sample of his sermons that he ever flew into real rages with his congregation. Not at all — and that was his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrible things to his crew in a tone so strangely mixed of fun and fury, with the fury seeming so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such odd invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides, all the while he himself looked so easy and lazy, handled his steering-oar so loungingly, and yawned so broadly — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, worked like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sorts of humorists whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous as to put all their subordinates on guard when it comes to obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's hogsheads of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what you came for. (Pull, my boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the arrival of these outlandish strangers at such a critical moment as the lowering of the boats had, not unreasonably, stirred a kind of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company. But Archy's supposed discovery had got around among them some time before, and though nobody had believed it then, it had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took the sharpest edge off their wonder; and so, what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for the strangers' appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious guessing — though the affair still left plenty of room for all kinds of wild conjectures about dark Ahab's exact part in the matter from the beginning. As for me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod in the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the cryptic hints of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meanwhile Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having edged farthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a sign of how powerful a crew was pulling him. Those tiger-yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone. Like five trip-hammers they rose and fell with regular strokes of strength, which every so often shot the boat along the water like a horizontal burst boiler out of a Mississippi steamer. As for Fedallah, who was seen pulling the harpooner's oar, he had thrown aside his black jacket and bared his chest, the whole of his body above the gunwale sharply outlined against the alternating dips of the watery horizon; while at the other end of the boat Ahab, one arm thrown half backward into the air like a fencer's, as if to counterbalance any tendency to trip, was seen steadily managing his steering oar as he had in a thousand boat-lowerings before the White Whale tore him. All at once the outstretched arm made a peculiar motion and then stayed fixed, while the boat's five oars were seen peaked all at once. Boat and crew sat motionless on the sea. Instantly the three spread-out boats behind paused on their way. The whales had irregularly sunk bodily down into the blue, giving no sign of the movement that could be seen from a distance, though Ahab, being closer, had observed it.
"Every man look out along his oars!" cried Starbuck. "You, Queequeg, stand up!"

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised box in the bow, the savage stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off toward the spot where the chase had last been sighted. Likewise, on the extreme stern of the boat, where it was also built up into a triangular platform level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and skillfully balancing himself against the jerking tosses of his chip of a craft, silently scanning the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far off, Flask's boat was also lying breathlessly still. Its commander was recklessly standing on top of the loggerhead, a stout sort of post rooted in the keel and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is no bigger than the palm of a man's hand, and standing on such a base as that, Flask seemed perched at the masthead of some ship that had sunk to all but her trucks, the caps at the very tops of her masts. But little King-Post was small and short, and at the same time little King-Post was full of a large and tall ambition, so that this loggerhead standpoint of his by no means satisfied King-Post.
"I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand on the gunwale to steady himself, swiftly slid to the stern, and then straightening up, volunteered his lofty shoulders as a pedestal.
"Good a masthead as any, sir. Will you mount?"
"That I will, and thank you very much, my fine fellow. Only I wish you were fifty feet taller."

Whereupon, planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic negro stooped a little and offered his flat palm to Flask's foot; then, putting Flask's hand on his hearse-plumed head and telling him to spring just as he himself should toss, with one skillful fling he landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And here now stood Flask, Daggoo with one lifted arm giving him a breastband to lean against and steady himself by.

At any time it is a strange sight to the novice to see with what wonderful, unconscious habit of skill the whaleman will keep upright in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Stranger still to see him giddily perched on the loggerhead itself in such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was more curious yet; for, holding himself up with a cool, indifferent, easy, unstudied, barbaric majesty, the noble negro rolled his fine form in harmony with every roll of the sea. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snowflake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. True, lively, tumultuous, showy little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but he did not add a single heave to the negro's lordly chest by it. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping on the living, magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, showed no such far-gazing anxieties. The whales might have made one of their regular soundings (their long, deep dives), not a temporary dive from mere fright; and if that were the case, Stubb, as was apparently his habit in such cases, was determined to while away the dragging interval with his pipe. He drew it from his hatband, where he always wore it at a slant like a feather. He loaded it and rammed the tobacco home with the end of his thumb; but he had barely struck his match across the rough sandpaper of his hand when Tashtego, his harpooner, whose eyes had been turned to windward like two fixed stars, suddenly dropped like light from his upright stance to his seat, crying out in a quick frenzy of hurry, "Down, down all, and give way! — there they are!"

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment — nothing but a troubled patch of greenish-white water, with thin, scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it and drifting diffusely off to leeward, like the confused spray blown from white rolling breakers. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it were, like the air over intensely heated plates of iron. Beneath this atmospheric waving and curling, and partly beneath a thin layer of water as well, the whales were swimming. Seen ahead of all the other signs, the puffs of vapor they spouted seemed their couriers running before them, their detached outriders flying ahead.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it seemed ready to outrun them. It flew on and on, like a mass of merging bubbles swept down a swift stream from the hills.

"Pull, pull, my good boys," said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but most intensely concentrated whisper to his men. The sharp fixed glance from his eyes, aimed straight ahead of the bow, seemed almost like two visible needles in two unerring binnacle compasses. He did not say much to his crew, nor did they say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals piercingly broken by one of his peculiar whispers — now harsh with command, now soft with pleading.

How different the loud little King-Post. "Sing out and say something, my hearties! Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys! Only do that for me, and I'll sign over my Martha's Vineyard plantation to you, boys — including wife and children, boys! Lay me on — lay me on! Oh Lord, Lord! I'll go stark, staring mad! See! See that white water!" And shouting like this, he pulled his hat from his head and stamped up and down on it; then, picking it up, he flicked it far off over the sea; and finally he took to rearing and plunging in the boat's stern like a crazed colt from the prairie.

"Look at that fellow now," Stubb drawled philosophically, following along at a short distance with his unlit pipe still mechanically clamped between his teeth. "He's got fits, that Flask has. Fits? Yes, give him fits — that's the very word — pitch fits into them. Merrily, merrily, hearts alive! Pudding for supper, you know — merry's the word. Pull, babes — pull, sucklings — pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling. Nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two — that's all. Take it easy — why don't you take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!"

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his — those are words best left out here, for you live under the blessed light of the evangelical land. Only the infidel sharks in the audacious seas may listen to such words, when, with a tornado brow and eyes of red murder and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. Flask's repeated, specific references to "that whale," as he called the imaginary monster that he declared was constantly teasing his boat's bow with its tail — these references of his were at times so vivid and lifelike that they would make one or two of his men snatch a fearful look over their shoulders. But this was against all rules; for the oarsmen must put out their eyes and ram a skewer through their necks, custom declaring that in these critical moments they must have no organs but ears and no limbs but arms.

It was a sight full of quick wonder and awe! The vast swells of the all-powerful sea; the surging, hollow roar they made as they rolled along the eight gunwales, like gigantic bowls on a boundless bowling green; the brief, suspended agony of the boat as it tipped for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves, which almost seemed to threaten to cut it in two; the sudden deep plunge into the watery glens and hollows; the keen spurring and goading to reach the top of the opposite hill; the headlong, sled-like slide down its other side — all these, with the cries of the headsmen and harpooners and the shuddering gasps of the oarsmen, and the wondrous sight of the ivory Pequod bearing down on her boats with outstretched sails, like a wild hen after her screaming brood — all this was thrilling.

Not the raw recruit who marches straight from his wife's arms into the fever heat of his first battle; not the dead man's ghost meeting the first unknown phantom of the other world — neither of these feels stranger or stronger emotions than the man who finds himself, for the first time, rowing into the charmed, churned-up circle of a hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water the chase churned up was growing more and more visible now, because the dull cloud-shadows thrown on the sea were getting darker. The jets of vapor had stopped blending together and slanted every which way, right and left; the whales seemed to be splitting their wakes apart. The boats spread farther from one another, Starbuck going after three whales that ran dead to leeward. We had our sail set now, and with the wind still rising we raced along, the boat tearing through the water so madly that the lee oars could hardly be worked fast enough to keep them from being ripped out of the rowlocks.
Soon we were running through a wide, drifting veil of mist. Neither ship nor boat to be seen.
"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding vapor shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

The boat was completely swamped but almost undamaged. We swam around it and gathered up the floating oars, lashed them across the gunwale, and scrambled back into our places. There we sat, knee-deep in the sea, with water over every rib and plank, so that to our eyes, gazing down, the boat hanging there in the water seemed like a coral boat that had grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves clashed their shields together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire on the prairie, in which we were burning without being consumed — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; you might as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, flying cloud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea ruled out any attempt to bail out the boat. The oars were useless for rowing, and now served as life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, Starbuck, after many failures, managed to light the lamp in the lantern; then, fixing it on a waif pole (the flagged pole used to mark a killed whale), he handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that feeble candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet and drenched through, shivering with cold, having given up hope of either ship or boat, we raised our eyes as dawn broke. The mist still lay spread over the sea, and the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg leaped to his feet and cupped his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, like the sound of ropes and yards that the storm had muffled until now. It came closer and closer; a huge, vague shape dimly parted the thick mist. In terror we all jumped into the sea as the ship finally loomed into view, bearing straight down on us, hardly more than her own length away.

From where we floated in the waves we saw the abandoned boat toss and gape for one instant under the ship's bows, like a chip of wood at the foot of a waterfall; then the huge hull rolled over it, and it vanished until it surfaced again, wallowing, astern. We swam for it again, were flung against it by the seas, and were finally picked up and brought safely on board. The other boats had cut loose from their fish before the squall reached them and had got back to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up for lost but was still cruising about, in case it might happen upon some sign of our death — an oar or a lance pole.
